perspective:
**Mason Hurley’s available information:**

- He is an accountant at a small community center and knows Martha Moua as a personal care aide colleague. Their relationship is professional and not close; they mainly interact about work.
- He reviewed the center’s financial reports and observed discrepancies: healthcare expenses seemed unusually high and inconsistent with usual spending patterns. This led him to suspect Martha might be mismanaging funds, and he felt suspicious and anxious.
- He initiated a discussion with Martha about the report, saying the numbers didn’t add up and pointing to the high healthcare expenses. He heard Martha say there was likely a reasonable explanation, that it might be a misentry, and that she would review and correct errors.
- After reviewing the report with Martha, he concluded the discrepancies were a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. He felt relieved and embarrassed. He apologized for his initial suspicion and said he should have asked her first. He heard Martha accept the apology, say errors happen, understand his thoroughness, and suggest double-checking entries next time.
- He then believed Martha was competent and that the real problem was inadequate financial management systems causing recurring clerical errors. He felt frustrated with the system but empathetic toward Martha. He proposed a new, more robust financial system, said he would draft a proposal, and asked for her input. He heard Martha agree and offer to help address the gaps.
- He drafted the proposal. He felt hopeful about its benefits but uncertain whether management would approve or implement it. He told Martha he had finished the draft, believed it would benefit operations, and was unsure how management would receive it. He heard Martha call it solid, encourage him to present confidently, and say the benefits were clear. He said he would prepare a detailed presentation and asked her to help gather data; he heard her agree.
- He presented the proposal to management. Afterward, he felt satisfied with his efforts but physically and mentally exhausted, believing he had done everything possible to advocate for the new system. He told Martha the presentation went well, he had done everything he could, and it was now up to management. He heard Martha praise him and suggest taking time off. He thanked her, said he would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, and hoped for good news. He heard Martha wish him a good break and offer help while he was away.
